evidence.claim: Along the Klamath and Trinity, a river road with a Bigfoot namesake
evidence.quote: State Route 96 (SR 96) is a state highway in the U.S. state of California that follows the Trinity and Klamath Rivers

evidence.claim: Along the Klamath and Trinity, a river road with a Bigfoot namesake
evidence.quote: The segment of SR 96 from Willow Creek to Happy Camp is designated as the Bigfoot Scenic Byway, a National Forest Scenic Byway

evidence.claim: Highway 96 follows the Klamath and Trinity rivers through Northern California.
evidence.quote: State Route 96 (SR 96) is a state highway in the U.S. state of California that follows the Trinity and Klamath Rivers between State Route 299 in Willow Creek and Interstate 5 near Yreka in Northern California.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service lists Bigfoot among three scenic byways through Klamath National Forest, describing its stretch along the Klamath from Happy Camp to Orleans.
evidence.quote: Three scenic byways run through the Klamath National Forest. The Bigfoot Scenic Byway runs along the Klamath River on Hwy 96 from Happy Camp to Orleans.

evidence.claim: The highway account identifies the longer Happy Camp–Willow Creek corridor as a National Forest Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: The segment of SR 96 from Willow Creek to Happy Camp is designated as the Bigfoot Scenic Byway, a National Forest Scenic Byway

evidence.claim: Along the lower Trinity, Hoopa Valley opens above Campbell Creek and narrows again at Bald Hill.
evidence.quote: The valley opens up above the confluence of Campbell Creek with the Trinity River and extends northward until it closes up again at the foot of Bald Hill.

evidence.claim: The route passes through Six Rivers National Forest between Orleans and Weitchpec, where Highway 169 branches away from Highway 96.
evidence.quote: At Weitchpec, the route intersects State Route 169 and turns northeast into the Six Rivers National Forest. The highway passes through Orleans

evidence.claim: The Forest Service gave this stretch of Highway 96 its Bigfoot name.
evidence.quote: Happy Camp is situated along the "Bigfoot Scenic Byway," an 89-mile stretch of California State Route 96 named by the United States Forest Service.

evidence.claim: Happy Camp gives the name a physical form with an 18-foot statue made from recycled metal.
evidence.quote: The town has an 18-foot-tall Bigfoot statue made of recycled metal.

evidence.claim: The road also links much older places: Orleans occupies the Karuk settlement of Panamnik, and Weitchpec is an ancestral Yurok village predating European contact.
evidence.quote: Orleans is within the historical territory of the Karuk Tribe of California. The original indigenous settlement was named Panamnik.

evidence.claim: Weitchpec is an ancestral Yurok village predating European contact
evidence.quote: Weitchpec is an ancestral Yurok village that long predates European contact.

evidence.claim: Gold-rush miners named Happy Camp during their early prosperity. The Karuk Tribe is headquartered there now, giving the town a present role beyond its mining-era name.
evidence.quote: Happy Camp was so named by California gold rush miners in the early days of prosperity.

evidence.claim: The Karuk Tribe is headquartered there now
evidence.quote: The Karuk Tribe is headquartered in Happy Camp.

evidence.claim: From Happy Camp, follow the Klamath toward Orleans and then Weitchpec.
evidence.quote: At Weitchpec, the route intersects State Route 169 and turns northeast into the Six Rivers National Forest. The highway passes through Orleans and turns more northerly after intersecting Salmon River Road. Passing through Happy Camp, SR 96 enters the Klamath National Forest.

evidence.claim: At the confluence, Highway 96 leaves the Klamath and follows the Trinity upstream through Hoopa to Willow Creek, where it meets Highway 299.
evidence.quote: SR 96 begins at a junction with State Route 299, the Trinity Highway, in Willow Creek. It heads north, following the Trinity River downstream through Hoopa, and exiting the Trinity National Forest near its confluence with the Klamath River at Weitchpec.

evidence.claim: An 18-foot Bigfoot made of recycled metal gives Happy Camp a visible link to the byway’s name.
evidence.quote: The town has an 18-foot-tall Bigfoot statue made of recycled metal.

evidence.claim: The Happy Camp Community Council also hosts the annual Bigfoot Jamboree.
evidence.quote: The Bigfoot Jamboree is an annual festival hosted by the Happy Camp Community Council.

evidence.claim: Gold-rush miners gave the town its English name during their early prosperity.
evidence.quote: Happy Camp was so named by California gold rush miners in the early days of prosperity.

evidence.claim: Its Karuk name is athithúf-vuunupma, and the Karuk Tribe has its headquarters here.
evidence.quote: Happy Camp (Karuk: athithúf-vuunupma)

evidence.claim: the Karuk Tribe has its headquarters here
evidence.quote: The Karuk Tribe is headquartered in Happy Camp.

evidence.claim: The town sits on the Klamath River where a network of creeks includes Elk Creek and Indian Creek.
evidence.quote: Happy Camp sits on the Klamath River and a nexus of creeks including Elk Creek, Little Grider Creek, Indian Creek

evidence.claim: Happy Camp is also an administrative base for the Forest Service’s Happy Camp/Oak Knoll Ranger Districts in Klamath National Forest.
evidence.quote: Happy Camp is the administrative site for the Happy Camp/Oak Knoll Ranger Districts of the Klamath National Forest.

evidence.claim: Happy Camp’s Bigfoot statue is 18 feet tall and made of recycled metal.
evidence.quote: The town has an 18-foot-tall Bigfoot statue made of recycled metal.

evidence.claim: Panamnik is the Karuk name for Orleans and the name of the original Indigenous settlement here.
evidence.quote: Orleans (formerly New Orleans Bar and Orleans Bar; Karuk: Panamnik)

evidence.claim: European-American miners called their settlement New Orleans Bar.
evidence.quote: The original indigenous settlement was named Panamnik.  When European-American miners arrived, they named their settlement New Orleans Bar.

evidence.claim: In 1855 it became Orleans Bar and the seat of Klamath County, a county that no longer exists.
evidence.quote: It was renamed Orleans Bar in 1855 when it became the county seat of the now-defunct Klamath County.

evidence.claim: Orleans lies within the historical territory of the Karuk Tribe of California.
evidence.quote: Orleans is within the historical territory of the Karuk Tribe of California.

evidence.claim: It is also within Six Rivers National Forest, with a district ranger’s office, on Highway 96 northeast of Weitchpec.
evidence.quote: It is located 12 miles (19 km) northeast of Weitchpec along State Route 96

evidence.claim: within Six Rivers National Forest, with a district ranger’s office
evidence.quote: The community is within the Six Rivers National Forest and contains a district ranger's office of the National Forest.

evidence.claim: The community is the nearest inhabited place to the remote site of the Patterson–Gimlin film of a purported Bigfoot, about ten miles northeast.
evidence.quote: Orleans is the nearest inhabited community to the site of the famous Patterson–Gimlin filming of a purported Bigfoot, which is in a remote area about 10 miles (16 km) northeast of Orleans.

evidence.claim: The Trinity joins the Klamath at Weitchpec, where Highways 96 and 169 also meet.
evidence.quote: Weitchpec is located in the northwestern part of the state at the confluence of the Klamath and Trinity Rivers, and the junction of State Highways 96 and 169.

evidence.claim: This ancestral Yurok village was known as Weitspus and was a major Yurok settlement before European contact.
evidence.quote: Weitchpec is an ancestral Yurok village that long predates European contact. It was originally known as Weitspus, and was considered a major settlement of the Yurok people.

evidence.claim: One temporary nineteenth-century name, Durkee’s Ferry, recalled the ferry Clark W. Durkee operated here in 1851.
evidence.quote: Durkee's Ferry recalls Clark W. Durkee, who operated a ferry at the place in 1851.

evidence.claim: Weitchpec is within the Yurok reservation and has a Yurok Tribal Office and Community Center.
evidence.quote: Weitchpec ( WETCH-pek; Karuk: Ansáfriik; Yurok: Wechpues, Wech) is an unincorporated village and CDP within the Yurok reservation

evidence.claim: has a Yurok Tribal Office and Community Center
evidence.quote: the Yurok Tribal Office and Community Center

evidence.claim: The village lay in Klamath County from 1851, then became part of Humboldt County after 1874.
evidence.quote: The settlement was first within the bounds of Trinity County, then in 1851 Klamath County and after 1874, Humboldt County.

evidence.claim: For the southbound drive, the confluence marks the change from following the Klamath to following the Trinity toward Hoopa.
evidence.quote: It heads north, following the Trinity River downstream through Hoopa, and exiting the Trinity National Forest near its confluence with the Klamath River at Weitchpec.
